newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cannes films leave critics wondering at quality.
newsitem.headline: Cannes films leave critics wondering at quality.

text.p: Cannes festival-goers packed their bags after a night of revelry on Monday, wondering aloud why its 50th edition was made up of so many uninspiring films reeking of violence and evil.

The jury led by French actress Isabelle Adjani rescued the jamboree with awards for a quirky Japanese film ("The Eel" by Shohei Imamura) and -- flagging its support -- for two directors who have tussled with censors, Iran's Abbas Kiarostami and Egypt's Youssef Chahine.

"The most exciting part of this festival was the wait for the awards, which had nothing of a foregone conclusion given an official selection with little relief despite its violent excesses," noted the French newspaper Le Figaro.
"Too black, morbid, sinister, and too much outrageous realism. Adjani's jury responded by rewarding films which celebrate life rather than death," the daily said.

Festival supremo Gilles Jacob had himself acknowledged that this anniversary selection reflected a downturn in quality worldwide, and critics speculated that the timing of the Cannes festival was also partly to blame.
Cannes has long stuck to its early May slot -- when the weather at the French Riviera resort is still too poor to fill hotels.
But the best European films are usually released in the autumn in time for the Christmas holidays, and the best American films come out in the summer when audiences are strongest.
Leading French critic Michel Ciment, who edits the film magazine Positif, also blamed the star-system which surfaced heavily at Cannes' birthday galas this year.

"Stars are getting too much attention at the expense of directors. The fact that someone like John Travolta can row with filmmaker Roman Polanski, tell him how the film should be made, and then abandon the set is typical," Ciment told Reuters.

Among the films rubbished most robustly in Cannes this year are "Assassin(s)" by France's Matthieu Kassovitz, a portrait of an ageing assassin which clumsily attempts to justify his trade, and "Funny Games" by Germany's Michael Haneke.
The latter is a no-holds-barred plunge into sadism as two youths torture a family both mentally and physically, occasionally turning to the camera to enlist the approval of the audience.

The few discoveries of this year's festival were outside the competition run -- a moving portrait of the late Marcello Mastroianni by his late partner ("I Remember"), Kenneth Branagh's splendid four-hour "Hamlet" and Manoel de Oliveira's "Journey to the Beginning of the World".

Adjani's jury surprised critics with a Golden Palm award to both Kiarostami, whose film "The Taste of the Cherry" almost missed the competition after Tehran authorities initially banned him from coming, and Imamura's "The Eel".

The French actress, who at the start of the festival had taken a stand for cinema freedom, announced a special 50th anniversary prize for Chahine, whose earlier movie "The Migrant" was banned after protests from Moslem fundamentalists.
Censorship overshadowed celebrations at the festival with China banning both Zhang Yimou and Zhang Yuan from showing films in Cannes this year.
The veteran Chahine was in competition with "Destiny", an ode to tolerance focussing on the life of a medieval philosopher, but Adjani made clear that his award was for his life's work.
Sean Penn and Kathy Burke won the best actor and best actress prizes respectively for Nick Cassavetes' "She's So Lovely" and Gary Oldman's first movie "Nil By Mouth" on London's East Enders.
